name: arc-collinear-gap-fill
description: Use when an ARC grid may fill gaps between matching markers.
---

# Fill gaps between collinear markers

For ARC-style grids with a uniform background, sparse marker cells, and evidence of a second fill color:

1. Inspect each row and column independently for marker cells of the same color.
2. Between consecutive markers along that row or column, replace only intervening background cells with the fill color.
3. Keep original markers and all cells outside those intervals unchanged. Do not connect diagonals unless examples explicitly show that rule.
4. If horizontal and vertical intervals overlap, the result is the same fill color there.
5. Build the output at the original dimensions and verify every changed cell is strictly between aligned same-color markers.
6. For large grids, generate the output programmatically from a parsed input rather than hand-transcribing it. Validate that the row count and every row width exactly match the input before submitting; a malformed row can make an otherwise correct transformation invalid.

This skill also covers the distinct ARC rule “recolor a stray/extension cell or region with 1”: do not assume collinear-gap filling merely because the grid is sparse. In the validated examples for this task family, a large uniform-background canvas has structured color-0/marker-2 or color-5/marker-8 motifs; only a particular trailing/right-side patch is recolored to 1. Example outcomes: (a) in a 12x10 grid with bg 6, marker 5, the 2x2 area at rows 3–4, cols 8–9 changes to 1; (b) in a 29x22 grid with bg 4, marker 0, a right-side 4x5 patch at rows 3–6, cols 17–21 changes to 1, while a similar repeated motif lower down does not; (c) in a 16x14 grid with bg 2, marker 0, only row 7, cols 8–13 changes to 1, not the similar lower motif; (d) a 9x14 case with bg 5 and horizontal 8 stripes on rows 0 and 4 had only the anomalous 5 at (0,13) recolored to 1. Thus determine which isolated/rightward region is selected by the demonstrations and preserve all other cells. A wrong attempt that applied generic gap-filling was incorrect. When the rule is unclear, request demonstrations rather than forcing the generic collinear fill heuristic.

Validated pattern: marker 8 on background 7, with fill color 3. A single-column test had marker 8 at rows 1, 2, and 5; rows 3 and 4 changed to 3. A 21x18 demonstration used markers 6 on background 1 and added 3 between collinear marker pairs across rows and columns, preserving markers and exterior background. Another demo used marker 4 on background 1, filling horizontal and vertical gaps between consecutive aligned markers with 3; cells beyond the outermost markers stayed background. A solved 26x19 case used marker 8 on background 0 with fill 3, confirming the same rule. A further 20x30 demo had target markers 5 on background 6; it changed intervening background cells to 3 between consecutive aligned 5s, while preserving 5s and all cells outside those intervals. This confirms the rule works with a non-7 background and the task's demonstrations should determine which colors play each role. For future tasks, infer marker, background, and fill colors from that task's demonstrations before applying the rule. A further 10x25 case used marker 6 on background 0 with fill 3; filling only the spaces between consecutive aligned 6s in each row and column solved it. A 9x26 demonstration used marker 0 on background 9 with fill 3; it confirmed the same rule: fill only intervals between consecutive same-color markers horizontally or vertically, preserving markers and exterior cells. A 10x20 case used marker 1 on background 9 with fill 3; fill only intervening cells between consecutive same-color markers in rows and columns, preserving all markers and outside cells. The completed test grid had markers at (0,6), (1,17), (2,11), (3,7),(3,15), (4,4),(4,9), (5,3),(5,11), (6,2),(6,9), (7,10),(7,11), and (8,12),(8,18), with zero-based coordinates; that solution was confirmed correct. The same-color straight-line interval rule applies when many marker pairs create extensive filled segments, while unbounded exterior cells remain unchanged.

A separate trailing-extension rule is confirmed by demos: on a uniform canvas, a horizontal stripe/marker segment whose right end is followed by background may have only the rightward tail recolored to 1. Carefully use the demo to identify WHICH row of a repeated motif is selected; do not recolor every stripe row merely because it ends before the edge. In one validated case, the chosen stripe row was the second/lower row of a two-row motif, and only background cells to the right of that row’s stripe were changed to 1. In another demo, the anomalous row had a long stripe ending at column 15 on an 18-wide grid, so only columns 16–17 became 1; a separate full-width stripe row remained unchanged. On the tested 24x15 grid with background 2 and stripes 7, only row index 14, columns 11–14, were recolored to 1; row index 13 (the aligned/upper stripe row) stayed unchanged even though its right side was background. This solved the case after earlier guesses that recolored both rows or the upper row were wrong. Thus preserve the exact motif row selection implied by demonstrations and change only the terminal tail, never interior background. Additional caution from a failed complex test: do not interpret every rightmost marker in a patterned block as a stripe. The confirmed demo tails were uninterrupted horizontal runs beginning at the left border; when a run has an interior background hole or starts inset from the left edge, do not automatically extend its right side. In repeated/multi-row motifs, use a further demo rather than broadly recoloring all rows that happen to end in background, and ensure output row widths remain exact. Another confirmed variant: background 8, stripe/object color 9, fill 1. A demo had a full-width row of 3s left unchanged, but in two separate rows with left-originating 3 segments that stopped early, every background cell to the right through the edge became 1. In the test, a compact two-row 9-pattern at the top ended at column 6, so background cells in columns 7–9 of both rows changed to 1; a lower two-row pattern that reached the right edge was unchanged (including internal gaps). Thus recolor the rightward tail only when the row’s 9-pattern terminates before the right edge, and preserve holes/internal background. More demonstrations confirm this row-tail rule with different background and stripe colors: background 2, stripe 6, fill 1 had one full-width stripe unchanged and a left-aligned partial stripe recolored to 1 from its right endpoint through the edge; background 3, stripe 0, fill 1 showed the same behavior, with the partial stripe row's tail recolored and a full-width stripe unchanged. In a 29x9 test with background 0 and stripe 4, the full-width stripe row stayed unchanged, while both partial left-aligned stripes (lengths 5 and 4) had their remaining cells to the right changed to 1. This establishes that all partial stripe rows are extended as 1 to the right edge; do not choose only one partial row when there are multiple, and do not change full-width rows. However, a 28x22 test with background 9 and foreground 4 had a different structured-pattern selection: only the terminal cell at column 21 was changed to 1 in rows 21 and 23 (zero-based); other rows ending in 4 immediately before background at the right edge remained unchanged. Thus do not blindly extend every row in a complex repeated pattern: use the demonstrated motif/block selection. # Triggered template stamping

Use when a uniform-background grid contains one distinctive, compact colored motif and scattered single-cell trigger markers.

1. From a demo, identify the exact template rectangle, trigger color, and which template coordinate aligns with each trigger. Do not assume the trigger aligns to the template center or corner.
2. For each trigger, translate the template in its demonstrated orientation so the anchor coordinate overlays the trigger. Recolor/overwrite the trigger with the template's value at that anchor.
3. Preserve the original template and unrelated cells. Add only the translated template values at the corresponding coordinates; keep areas outside the translated rectangle unchanged. Verify edge clipping behavior from demos if a stamp would cross the grid boundary.
4. Apply at every matching trigger if demos show all triggers are used. Preserve dimensions and exact row widths.

Confirmed variant: the input template may be a 1x5 horizontal motif `[2,1,2,2,6]`, with sparse trigger cells `3`. The trigger aligns with the template's third cell (zero-based offset `(0,2)`), and the motif is copied horizontally in the same orientation at every trigger; the trigger is replaced with `2`.
